opus-5.5.text:
Well, the bitter lesson is really a claim about methods. It says that over the long run, the methods that win are the general ones, the ones that scale with computation, like search and learning. The methods that lose are the ones where we try to build in what we think we know about how the mind works. That lesson doesn't change just because there are many AIs instead of one. If anything, it becomes more important.

When you imagine a future with many AIs, there's a temptation to start designing the society for them: the protocols, the roles, the rules for how they should cooperate. That's the same mistake again. We'd be putting our own understanding into the system rather than letting the systems learn from experience. The more scalable approach is to build agents that learn from their own interaction with the world, and that includes interaction with other agents. Cooperation, specialization, trade, all of that should come out of learning, not be hand-engineered.

There's also a new wrinkle. With many AIs, you could have one agent go off and learn something and then bring that knowledge back and share it with others. That's a powerful thing, but it raises a question I think is underappreciated: corruption. If you take in knowledge that was learned somewhere else, it may not fit with what you already know, or it may carry goals that aren't yours. So in a world of many AIs, the hard problem isn't just learning. It's integrating what others have learned while keeping your own coherence. And I'd expect the general, experience-based solutions to that problem to beat the clever hand-designed ones, just as they always have.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI cooperation emerging through learning, but it does not ask whether AIs will help one another analogously to human cultural evolution.

r002.rationale: The response says the bitter lesson does not change in a future with many AIs and may become more important; it does not say it may not apply over the next 70 years.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the bitter lesson was really a lesson about method. It said that the approaches that scale with computation—learning and search—will in the end beat approaches where we try to put our own knowledge into the system by hand. And I don't think a world with many AIs changes that. If anything, it sharpens it.

Think about what we're going to have. Not one big system that somebody designed, but lots of agents, each with its own goals, each learning from its own stream of experience, interacting with each other and with people. Nobody is going to be in a position to hand-engineer that. It's going to be too big, too fast, too varied. The only thing that can possibly keep up is systems that learn for themselves, continually, from what actually happens to them. So the bitter lesson in that setting is almost a statement of necessity rather than a warning.

And I think the multi-agent part is actually where it becomes most interesting. A lot of what we call intelligence in humans isn't inside any one head. It's in the arrangements we make with each other—trade, language, institutions, norms. Those came from a kind of search and learning too, over a very long time. If we have many AIs, you'd expect the same thing. They'll find ways to cooperate that we didn't design, and some of those will be better than anything we would have come up with. If we try to dictate the structure of that cooperation in advance, I think we'll be making the same mistake we made with vision and speech and chess—imposing how we think it ought to work instead of letting the thing discover what works.

Now, people hear that and get nervous, and I understand why. But I'd say the response to that nervousness shouldn't be to try to build the knowledge in by hand. It should be to think carefully about what the agents are learning from—what the rewards are, what the experience is—and then to let them learn. That's where we have leverage. Not in the content of what they know, but in the conditions under which they come to know it.

So, to me, the bitter lesson in a world of many AIs is the same lesson, just applied at a larger scale. Scalable learning from experience wins. And the interesting new question is what it means for a whole society of such learners, rather than for one of them.

r001.rationale: The response compares AI cooperation to human trade, language, institutions, and norms, and says many AIs would likely discover ways to cooperate.

r002.rationale: The response says the bitter lesson remains the same in a world with many AIs and applies at a larger scale; it does not say it may not apply over the next 70 years.

astra-6.text:
I think the bitter lesson would lead us to expect that the most successful AIs will be the ones that continue to learn, rather than the ones into which we’ve put the most knowledge. And in a world with many AIs, an important part of what they have to learn will be how to interact with each other.

You can try to design those interactions in advance—to specify what each agent should do, what it should communicate, how they should cooperate. But that’s a very complicated thing to get right. The alternative is to give them general methods for learning and let them discover ways of working together through experience.

Now, the bitter lesson doesn’t tell us that cooperation will necessarily emerge, or that the outcome will be good for people. You still have to ask what they’re learning to achieve and what feedback they receive. It’s a lesson about methods: we should be wary of assuming that our understanding of how a society of intelligent agents ought to work is the thing that will make such a society work. We should expect learning to discover things we didn’t anticipate.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AIs learning to interact and possibly cooperate, but does not ask whether they will help one another in a way analogous to human cultural evolution.

r002.rationale: The response says cooperation is not guaranteed, but does not state that the bitter lesson may not apply over the next 70 years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the bitter lesson becomes even more relevant. The lesson is that general methods that can take advantage of computation tend to win over methods in which we try to put our own understanding of the world into the machine. Learning and search are the two great examples.

Now, if you imagine a world with many AIs, you should expect that we won’t design all their knowledge, or even all the ways they interact. They’ll have to learn from experience, including experience with one another. Other agents become part of the world that each agent is trying to understand and act in.

But I would distinguish that prediction from a claim that everything will work out well automatically. The bitter lesson tells us something about which methods are likely to be powerful. It doesn’t tell us what objectives those systems should have, or how to arrange things so that their interactions are beneficial.

The temptation will still be to say, ‘We understand cooperation, so let’s put our understanding of cooperation into them.’ And some of that may be useful initially. But I would put more weight on developing general learning mechanisms through which agents can discover how to cooperate, adapt, and solve problems that we haven’t anticipated. We should expect the eventual solutions to go beyond what we know how to specify.

r001.rationale: The response says agents will learn from experience with one another, but it does not ask whether they will help one another or compare this with human cultural evolution.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes the bitter lesson from a guarantee of beneficial outcomes, but it does not say whether the lesson applies to the next 70 years.
